Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-21 16:00 PT

Attendees: Jamie Ortiz (Redwood AE), Aria Chen (Redwood SE), Markus Vale (Lambda CTO), Priya Rao (Head of Security), Ethan Cole (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Quick vendor security review focused on encryption at rest and in transit, KMS/BYOK options, HSM-backed keys, key rotation and access controls. Customer emphasized data residency requirements and audit logs retention. Action items: share architecture diagram, SOC2 artifacts, schedule key rotation workshop, propose PoC configuration.

Topics: encryption at rest, envelope encryption, BYOK workflow, HSM vs cloud KMS, key rotation cadence, audit trail and SIEM integration, cross-region key replication, SSO/RBAC mapping to key use, split-knowledge for key custodians.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie: Alright everyone thanks for joining. sounds like we have Priya and Markus and Ethan from Lambda, thanks for blocking time. I'm Jamie Ortiz, AE on the account, and Aria from our SE team will run most of the tech discussion.
[00:08] Aria: hi all, quick agenda — review how Redwood handles encryption in transit and at rest, options for bringing your own key (BYOK), HSM-backed key storage, and then Q&A. Keep it practical — we can sketch an architecture for the PoC.
[00:17] Markus: thanks. high level we want to confirm that customer managed keys are possible, that keys never leave our control, and that logs show exactly who used what key and when. also need to verify data residency — some PII must stay in eu-west-1.
[00:31] Priya: yes, and for compliance we'll need SOC2 artifacts, KMS access policies, rotation proofs, and ideally a separation of duties for key management.
[00:39] Ethan: plus we want to understand what Redwood's runtime stores in memory vs encrypted cache, e.g., the KV cache — sometimes transcripts say K-V, sorry, kv cache — and whether long lived tokens persist.
[00:52] Aria: great, good checklist. short answers up front: we support encryption in transit TLS 1.2/1.3, all data at rest is encrypted by default. For customer-managed keys we integrate with cloud KMS providers (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS) and we also support HSM-backed keys via BYOK where the key material is generated or imported into an HSM.
[01:12] Jamie: i'll hand off to Aria for the architecture dive.
[01:15] Aria: ok, walk through — common pattern is envelope encryption. payloads are encrypted with a data key (DEK) at the runtime level; that DEK is then wrapped by a Key Encryption Key (KEK) which is stored in your KMS. This keeps the bulk data encrypted and limits KMS calls to key wrap/unwrap. it also reduces egress of plaintext keys.
[01:33] Markus: so the DEK is ephemeral and lives only in memory of the serving process?
[01:38] Aria: yes, exactly. DEKs are generated per-session or per-shard depending on policy. They live in the process memory and in the GPU address space while needed; our runtime uses secure memory heuristics and immediate zeroization after use where possible. we also can use hardware-backed mlock-like protections on dedicated hosts.
[01:55] Priya: how about rotation and key versioning? compliance expects to see rotation events and proof that old keys can't decrypt new records.
[02:03] Aria: KMS providers give versioned keys. rotation is achieved by using a new KEK for wrapping new DEKs; older wrapped DEKs remain decodable by older KEK versions unless you rewrap them. We recommend a rotation cadence (e.g., 90 days) and periodic rewrap of stored DEKs for long lived objects. we can provide scripts and a rewrap runbook as part of the PoC.
[02:25] Ethan: rewrap sounds potentially heavy for large storage — any optimization?
[02:29] Aria: yes — you can keep object headers pointing at the KEK version used to wrap the DEK. Only when keys are compromised or after a policy window you rewrap. For high-throughput caches we rely on TTL-based cache eviction to limit rewrap surface. also, if you use HSMs with key wrapping acceleration there's less overhead.
[02:47] Markus: can you explain HSM-backed vs cloud-managed KMS? we want FIPS compliance and hardware roots of trust.
[02:54] Aria: sure — cloud KMS like AWS KMS usually uses HSMs behind the service and is FIPS-validated on the vendor side. BYOK with an HSM means you retain control of key import/generation into the HSM instance you manage or that the cloud vendor provides in a dedicated tenancy. Some customers prefer dedicated HSM appliances (e.g., Luna, Thales) if they require split-knowledge and offline key generation.
[03:14] Priya: split-knowledge — can Redwood support a model where key custodians approve unwraps or generation? we need separation of duty for production keys.
[03:23] Aria: Redwood itself doesn't hold your key plaintext. For split-knowledge workflows you would implement approvals in your KMS/HSM. We support an integration where key usage calls (Decrypt/Unwrap) can be proxied through a policy layer — for example a short lived workflow where an operator triggers a rewrap or a key unwrap and that call is gated by your approval system. We can log the request and response metadata into your audit sink.
[03:45] Jamie: just to be clear — Redwood's control plane never sees your unwrapped data keys for BYOK flows, right?
[03:50] Aria: correct. in BYOK, the KEK stays in your KMS; Redwood issues key-wrap/unwrap calls to your KMS endpoint within your VPC or via a private connection. we do not store plaintext KEKs or DEKs.
[03:59] Markus: ok that helps. next, data residency — we have EU-only PII. If we deploy Redwood in us-east for latency, can we ensure data-at-rest for those objects remains in eu-west?
[04:11] Aria: yes. you can scope storage and key usage by region. Best practice: host the workloads and storage where the data must remain. For hybrid setups, you can configure routing policies so requests touching EU PII route to eu hosts, and those nodes use the eu KMS. We also support per-tenant metadata tagging so the storage layer enforces residency.
[04:29] Priya: how do you enforce logs residency? CloudTrail goes to a bucket — we want audit logs for key usage to remain in-region and be retained for 7 years for audit.
[04:39] Aria: you can configure your KMS to write CloudTrail logs to an S3 bucket in the region with lifecycle policies. Additionally, Redwood can stream its own access logs to your SIEM via a private endpoint in the region or to your S3 bucket. We'll provide a reference CloudFormation/Terraform to wire this up.
[04:54] Ethan: are the logs tamper-evident? we need chain-of-custody for keys and usage events.
[04:59] Aria: CloudTrail has immutability features if you use Object Lock and write-once buckets. For stronger proofs, some customers publish signed log digests to a separate digest store. We can also configure syslog forwarding with signed entries.
[05:12] Jamie: there was a question earlier about runtime memory — do you persist any PII in plaintext to disk?
[05:17] Aria: No, plaintext is not persisted to disk. The runtime may temporarily hold decrypted tokens or prompt context in memory for inference, but we zeroize and rely on ephemerality. On Dedicated instances you can opt into encrypted swap, and on Private installs you can enable kernel-level mlock to prevent swapping sensitive pages to disk.
[05:33] Priya: ok, kernel-level protections are good. what about network isolation — do you have options for VPC endpoints so KMS calls don't traverse public nets?
[05:41] Aria: yes — you can set up a VPC endpoint or a private link. We support private connectivity patterns: AWS PrivateLink, VPC peering, or customer VPN/direct connect for on-prem HSM. Key calls remain within these private channels when configured.
[05:55] Markus: what about key lifecycle operations via API — can we see every Decrypt/GenerateDataKey call with caller identity and which model route triggered it? We need traceability linking key use to model versions and request IDs.
[06:08] Aria: we attach request IDs and model route metadata to calls and you'll see that in CloudTrail or our audit hooks. We also provide a mapping of token-level events to key operations in the Console logs so you can cross-reference request IDs.
[06:21] Ethan: any PII leak risk via logs? e.g., prompt text included in traces?
[06:26] Aria: by default we redact prompt text from export logs unless you opt into debug tracing. You can also route logs through a scrubbing layer in your SIEM to remove sensitive fields.
[06:36] Priya: SSO/RBAC — can we map our SAML roles to Redwood roles and also to KMS key policies? We want principle of least privilege where only certain service accounts can perform Unwrap operations.
[06:47] Jamie: yep, Aria will explain the RBAC mapping.
[06:50] Aria: Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. For key usage, the best practice is to create dedicated service roles in your KMS that Redwood uses to call Unwrap; those roles are scoped to specific keys and operations. On the Redwood side we map your SAML groups to internal roles so only allowed routes or projects can call into the KMS.
[07:05] Markus: is there a way to enforce per-request MFA for especially sensitive unwraps?
[07:09] Aria: Some KMS setups support an external approval flow with an MFA requirement in front of the key. Alternatively you can implement an approval workflow in an intermediary service that only issues temporary credentials to Redwood after an operator approves.
[07:21] Priya: audit/alerts — we want to be alerted on anomalous key usage patterns. Does Redwood integrate with detection rules?
[07:27] Aria: yes we emit events; we can push to your SIEM and you can run correlation rules. We also have optional rules in the Console for threshold-based alerts — e.g., x unwraps per minute triggers an alert — but for full investigation you usually wire events into Splunk/Elastic/Datadog.
[07:41] Ethan: latency concern — if every request needs a KMS roundtrip for unwrap at inference time, that could add ms tens to latency. How do you keep p99 down?
[07:50] Aria: that's why envelope encryption is recommended. Short lived DEKs are cached per-node in memory so you don't call KMS per token; you call only to unwrap when the DEK is first needed or on rewrap. For low-latency workloads we use prefix caching and keep DEKs hot for the session, with an eviction TTL that balances security and latency.
[08:07] Markus: what about burst handling — if we have a sudden spike, do you risk hitting KMS API limits?
[08:13] Aria: yes KMS has API rate limits. Options: pre-warm DEKs, set up regional fallback keys, or ask your KMS provider for quota increase. For Dedicated customers we offer an edge cache layer to reduce KMS calls. We'll include patterns in the PoC doc.
[08:28] Priya: liability — if keys are compromised in transit or at the provider, who is responsible? we need contractual language in the DPA.
[08:35] Jamie: legal will work with you on DPA language. technically, BYOK reduces vendor access to key material; for shared keys Redwood is responsible to protect keys per agreement. We'll loop in legal and security.
[08:46] Priya: good. also want to confirm FIPS and PCI considerations for cardholder data if we decide to pass partial PANs to the model.
[08:54] Aria: we can support FIPS 140-2 validated HSMs and suggest tokenization for PANs — avoid sending raw card data to models if possible. We can work with your PCI assessor to map controls.
[09:07] Markus: ok can you show a quick schematic of the envelope flow and where logs are emitted?
[09:11] Aria: sure, i'll share the whiteboard in a sec. (screen share) Here's the flow: client -> Redwood API -> routing to eu nodes -> runtime decrypts with DEK in memory -> DEK wrapped by KEK in your KMS -> KMS logs CloudTrail -> Redwood emits request metadata to your SIEM.
[09:31] Markus: visual looks fine. what about key import vs key generation — we want keys generated in an HSM we control, not imported.
[09:39] Aria: you can choose both. For highest assurance generate the key inside your HSM (GenerateKey) and never export the private material. For cloud KMS you can request an import token or use key material that never leaves the HSM depending on provider features. We'll document provider-specific steps.
[09:53] Ethan: can we do offline key ceremony with split knowledge and then upload a wrapped KEK to the cloud?
[09:58] Aria: yes that's common. You perform an offline generation and use import tokens to put a wrapped key into the KMS. The KMS can then use that as KEK for envelope decrypt/wrap operations. Important: track key lineage and import timestamps in your inventory.
[10:12] Priya: retention — if we delete a dataset, can we prove the ciphertext is unrecoverable?
[10:18] Aria: if you delete the wrapped DEKs and the KEK is destroyed or rotated and rewrapped with a new KEK that doesn't have access to older DEKs, then ciphertext is unrecoverable. You should combine delete of data objects and key material/rewrap logic for crypto-retention policies.
[10:31] Markus: is there a built-in key destruction API you can call to make destruction auditable?
[10:36] Aria: KMS providers expose key schedule deletion APIs with time delays (e.g., scheduled deletion). For HSM appliances there's usually an admin operation to zeroize key material with tamper-evidence logs. We'll capture that in the runbook.
[10:48] Ethan: question about telemetry — we want to capture per-request model version and key version so we can do forensics later. how verbose are Redwood logs by default?
[10:55] Aria: default logs include request id, route/model id, node id, and a key operation id. We don't include prompt text by default. For PoC we can bump the verbosity in a controlled environment to include additional metadata for diagnostics.
[11:08] Priya: okay. vendors — you mentioned Anthropic and others earlier — do any competitors do BYOK better or differently?
[11:15] Jamie: some competitors offer managed keys only and don't support customer HSM import. others have stronger integrations with specific clouds. We can outline differences in the follow-up doc.
[11:25] Markus: let's talk about performance derisking for the PoC. what's the smallest configuration that demonstrates BYOK unwrap and low latency?
[11:32] Aria: a single-node Dedicated instance in eu-west with a KMS key scoped to that project, pre-warmed DEK cache, and CloudTrail logging is usually sufficient. We'll measure p50/p95/p99 and include network latency to KMS in the baseline.
[11:45] Ethan: will you provide scripts to spin up the PoC infra?
[11:48] Aria: yes Terraform + example policies.
[11:51] Priya: non-technical question — if an auditor asks for proof we rotated keys on schedule, what artifacts can you export?
[11:58] Aria: we can provide time-stamped CloudTrail events for KMS GenerateKey/RotateKey/DisableKey, key version metadata, and Redwood-side audit logs showing the rewrap operations and request ids.
[12:10] Markus: is Redwood's console considered a control plane that could be attacked to abuse key calls? what's the mitigation?
[12:17] Aria: the console is separate from the runtime. access to the control plane is protected by SAML SSO, 2FA controls, and RBAC. For enterprise customers we support private control plane options that live in your network. Also, by using BYOK and restricting KMS roles to VPC endpoints you reduce blast radius from console compromise.
[12:38] Priya: about private control plane — how does that affect log shipping and upgrades?
[12:43] Aria: in private deployments you manage upgrades through an agreed process; log shipping is to your endpoints. We'll coordinate upgrade windows and provide signed release artifacts.
[12:53] Jamie: quick check — any blockers so far?
[12:56] Priya: just one: we need an explicit design for split-knowledge approvals and evidence that the runtime won't cache key plaintext to disk.
[13:04] Aria: noted — we'll add a design section and runtime mem-safety notes.
[13:07] Markus: thanks. one more question — cross-region replication of keys for DR: how do you recommend?
[13:13] Aria: replicate keys by creating key material in each region or use multi-region KMS keys where supported. Ensure replication is audited and access is region-scoped. For DR, pre-warm DEKs in standby nodes so failover won't cause mass KMS unwrapping.
[13:27] Ethan: anything else on regulatory constraints? Priya?
[13:30] Priya: we'll need to map to ISO 27001 controls and our internal SOC mapping. If you can provide RFC-style control mappings that help.
[13:38] Aria: yes, we have a controls mapping doc; we'll attach it.
[13:41] Jamie: great. let's move to specific open items and next steps.
[13:44] Markus: first, PoC config and infra as discussed. second, please send SOC2, penetration test summary, and the architecture diagram. third, schedule the key rotation workshop with Aria. fourth, provide example KMS policies scoped down to least privilege.
[13:58] Jamie: will do. we'll also include a guide on CloudTrail + S3 immutability and a sample SIEM alert ruleset.
[14:05] Priya: timeline — we want to get legal and PCI involved; can you give us a timeline for PoC? 3 weeks for initial config?
[14:11] Aria: 2-3 weeks typical for a minimal PoC with a dedicated node and KMS setup. We'll aim for 2 weeks and adjust depending on approvals.
[14:18] Markus: ok that works.
[14:20] Jamie: wrapping up — i'll send calendar invites for the workshop and PoC kickoff. thanks all.
[14:26] Priya: thanks.

[14:30] End of recording.
